data.title: SpaceX Stock Climbs Toward IPO Price As Musk Floats $128 Quintillion Value
data.description:
TLDR

  • SpaceX (SPCX) rose about 3% premarket Friday to $131.13, under its $135 IPO price.

  • The FCC approved up to 1 million satellites to work as orbital data centers.

  • Musk said SpaceX could be worth $128 quintillion, but gave no time frame.

  • Micron, Sandisk and Anthropic posted bigger or similar gains on the day.

  • Analysts on TipRanks rate the stock Strong Buy, with a $265 average target.

SpaceX (SPCX) stock rose about 3% in premarket trading on Friday as tech names rallied on Black Friday. It traded at $131.13, less than $4 below its $135 IPO price.

The stock has struggled since its June debut. Fears that AI spending could slow as interest rates rise have weighed on it.

The latest push came on Wednesday, when the FCC approved plans for up to 1 million satellites to work as data centers in orbit. The agency said the decision would advance American leadership in space and artificial intelligence.

Elon Musk added his own forecast in a post on X on Thursday. He said SpaceX could be worth about $128 quintillion if it helps people live on more than one planet and taps even a small part of the Sun’s energy.

He also urged holders to keep their stock. Musk said both goals would be very hard to meet and gave no time frame.

Doing the Math on $128 Quintillion

The figure works out to roughly one million times the world economy. The IMF puts that economy at about $128 trillion.

SpaceX was worth about $1.7 trillion at Wednesday’s close. Reaching $128 quintillion would mean a gain of roughly 75 million times, which is a lot of zeros.

The post is not a formal price target. It also does not show how much cash the plans could earn.

Other stocks moved more on Friday. Micron rose 6.2% and Sandisk jumped 11%, while Anthropic, SpaceX’s biggest customer, climbed 3.1%.

The Deadlines Behind the Satellites

The planned satellites are called Starmind. They would act as data centers and use lasers to pass data to one another.

SpaceX must put its first working satellite in orbit by November 2033. It must reach 100,000 satellites by November 2035, with the full fleet due by November 2040.

Earlier this month, Musk said SpaceX ordered solar gear from Germany’s Singulus Technologies. The goal is 100 gigawatts in annual output.

The plan still faces risks, including launch costs and space debris. SpaceX also needs to prove the system can make money.

SpaceX posted $14.57 billion in third-quarter fiscal 2026 sales, up 161% from a year ago. Net income was $4.4 billion, compared with a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.

On TipRanks, SPCX holds a Strong Buy rating, with 28 Buys, six Holds and one Sell. The average price target is $265, about 108% above Wednesday’s $127.44 close.

Submitting a card application also leaves existing staking positions, lock-up periods, Dynamic Reward Rates, boosters, and stToken balances unchanged.

data.title: Indian Rupee Corrects Further As Renewed Hormuz Risk Lifts Oil Prices
data.description:
The Indian Rupee (INR) extends its correction further against the US Dollar (USD) on Friday. The USD/INR pair recovers further to near 92.75 as a sharp recovery in oil prices weighs on the Indian currency.

On Friday, the MCX Crude Oil contract expiring on December 18 extends its winning streak for the fourth trading day, rising 1.5% to near Rs. 8,000.

Currencies from economies, such as India, which rely heavily on oil imports to meet their energy needs, tend to underperform in a high-oil-price environment.

Oil gains deepen as Strait of Hormuz risks intensify

Strategists at Scotiabank stress that the latest advance in crude is more than a routine bounce, arguing that “the gains are important, notable, and reflect the renewed barrage of worrisome headlines suggesting an intensification of Iranian strikes on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz.” They point to this escalation in geopolitical tension as a key driver of the move, reinforcing the market’s sensitivity to any disruption risks along this critical shipping corridor.

Continued FII buying likely limits INR’s downside

The continuous inflow of overseas funds into the Indian stock market will likely keep the downside in the Indian Rupee limited. So far in November, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) have remained net buyers on all complete trading days and raised their stake worth Rs. 1,27,944.79 crore.

The interest of FIIs in the Indian stock market has started looking beyond the global Artificial Intelligence (AI) trade, following the victory of Democrats in United States (US) midterm elections and corporate governance issues in giant chipmaker Nvidia.

RBI is almost certain to hike rates next week

Analysts at Deutsche Bank said, “With Consumer Price Index (CPI) now above tolerance band, underlying inflation broadening and real GDP growth likely to remain above 7% despite West Asia crisis, the bank expects Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to continue tightening.” Reuters reported. The bank added that there are also risks of a bigger RBI Repo Rate hike on December 4.

Technical Analysis: USD/INR finds cushion near 92.20

In the daily chart, USD/INR trades at 92.75, keeping a bearish near-term tone as it remains under the 20-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) at 93.51. The pair’s inability to reclaim this overhead EMA suggests rallies are still being capped by short-term trend resistance, while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 33.74 has bounced from oversold territory but stays below the mid-50s area, hinting at only modest stabilization rather than a decisive reversal.

On the topside, immediate resistance is located at the 20-day EMA near 93.51, and a sustained break above this level would be needed to ease current downside pressure and open the door for a broader corrective rebound. Looking down, the November 25 low at 92.18 is the key support level.

data.title: Expect A Fiscal Year 2027 Initial Freeze In Military Spending
data.description:
Zero of Twelve Fiscal Year 2027 Funding Bills Have Passed Congress. Democrats take control January 3.

Fiscal Year 2027 Deadline Is December 11. Zero Chance.

Congress still haven’t enacted a single one of the 12 regular appropriations bills for FY2027.

The government is currently running on a continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103) that expires at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on December 11.

What to Expect

A full-year set of bills before the deadline is not happening. But this is the pattern, not the exception.

Since FY1977, Congress has needed at least one continuing resolution in all but three years.

Expect another continuing resolution, probably a short one that kicks the can into the next Congress.

How Often Are Zero of Twelve Spending Bills This Late?

In 21 of the 49 fiscal years since FY1977, Congress enacted zero regular appropriations bills by October 1.

Of those 21, 16 occurred after FY1997 (the last year all bills were finished on time).

In recent decades, starting the year with zero bills enacted has been the norm, not the exception. Since roughly 2011–2012, it has happened in most years.

What’s Different This Time?

In the 2026 midterms (November 3), Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate:

  • House: Democrats ended up with roughly 259 seats (their largest majority since 1992), Republicans ~173.

  • Senate: Democrats 56 (including 2 independents who caucus with them), Republicans 44. They flipped 9 seats.

Republicans currently hold both chambers in the lame-duck 119th Congress.

On January 3, 2027, that fully reverses when the 120th Congress convenes. The presidency remains with Trump, so it becomes divided government, but with Democrats holding the legislative branch.

Why this Changes the FY2027 Funding Dynamics

The underlying procedural failure (zero of 12 regular bills enacted this late) is not unusual.

What is different is the incentive structure created by the total switch:

  • Democrats have little reason to cut a full-year deal now. Waiting until January gives them control of both appropriations committees and much more leverage over spending levels, policy riders, and restrictions.

  • Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray and others have publicly preferred a short-term CR that pushes the real negotiations into the new Congress.

  • Republicans are trying to lock in as much as they can (especially on defense) while they still have the majority, but they need Democratic votes in the Senate to do almost anything.

  • Result: Stronger-than-usual pressure for another short CR rather than finishing any full-year bills before December 11.

How this Compares to Other Years

Lame-duck sessions after midterms often have some of these dynamics when control is about to change, but a full flip of both chambers at once is less common.

The fact that Democrats are about to take full control of Congress in January makes it less likely than usual that the current Republican majorities will finish any of the FY2027 bills on their own terms before the deadline.

Military Spending

Most reporting and lawmakers treat a full-year Defense appropriations bill (or any of the other 11) as very unlikely in the lame duck.

The expected outcome is another short-term CR, possibly running into early 2027.

The White House has already requested various defense “anomalies” (exceptions) for the next CR, including money for Trump’s Golden Dome idea, Trump-class battleships, and other programs.

The separate $350 billion reconciliation package the administration wanted for extra defense spending is widely described as dead or close to it.

Chris Coons (the top Democrat on Senate Defense Appropriations) said the final number will be closer to $1 trillion and will almost certainly be settled next year under the new Democratic majorities.

What Hegseth and the White House Requested

About $1.5 trillion total for FY2027 national defense:

  • Roughly $1.15 trillion in the regular (discretionary) base budget

  • Plus $350 billion through a separate reconciliation bill

This was framed as a roughly 42–44% increase over prior-year levels. It was the largest single-year defense request in modern history.

What Congress Has Moved

  • House Appropriations Committee Defense bill: ~$1.072 trillion

  • Senate Republicans’ Draft: ~$1.1 trillion

  • NDAA versions: roughly $1.14–1.15 trillion (authorization only – not funding)

The $350 billion reconciliation package is widely described as dead or extremely unlikely in the lame-duck session.

What’s Likely

Hegseth and the White House asked for $1.5 trillion. The near-term reality is another continuing resolution that largely freezes funding near existing levels.

Any final full-year number will almost certainly be set in 2027 after Democrats take control of both chambers, and it is unlikely to reach the full $1.5 trillion request.

Understanding “Initial“

My headline says “Expect a Fiscal Year 2027 Initial Freeze in Military Spending”

Unfortunately, budget compromises nearly always are more of this for more of that.

Republicans want more military spending and offer more social spending to get it. History says expect more of the same.

However, the combination 56 Democrat Senators and 259-260 Democrat House seats changes the dynamics a bit.

Note that Republicans failed to pass much legislation in the past two because a small minority of Republicans could block legislation.

The next Congress will be vastly different. Senate and House leaders cannot be held hostage by a few votes.

However, Trump has a veto. To get things Democrats want, they will need to either compromise or wait until 2028.

That compromise dynamic is not yet clear. But Democrats can force the issue on many bills. Trump will own the political consequences if he vetoes popular measures.

Either way, items such as Golden Dome and the proposed Trump-class warships look more likely to land on the ash heap of unfunded ideas.

Otherwise it’s wait-and-see, but the balance of leverage has clearly shifted.

data.title: Money Matters
data.description:
Among the world’s most important central banks, inflation is currently the main concern. Even in those parts of the world where the economy is weak, monetary policy is being driven primarily by the view that inflation is too high. This likely will change during the first half of next year, when the combination of lower inflation rates and slower economic growth rates causes economic weakness to become the overriding concern and prompts a major shift towards monetary easing. For at least another two months, however, it’s likely that central banks will be tightening the proverbial monetary screws and the ‘liquidity’ backdrop will remain problematic for most assets. One important aspect of the liquidity backdrop is the monetary inflation rate, as illustrated for some countries/regions by the monthly charts displayed below.

The latest data from the Fed indicate a year-over-year True Money Supply (TMS) growth rate (monetary inflation rate) of around 7% for the US. This means that US monetary inflation has returned to near its long-term average after the massive swings of 2020-2023. With the Fed focused on the inflation bounce of the past few months — an inflation bounce caused mainly by war-related supply issues — and with the US housing market in the doldrums, the US monetary inflation rate probably will fall over the next few months. However, by the second quarter of next year, the US monetary trend probably will turn upward as the Fed reacts to the declining price inflation and economic weakness that suddenly have appeared in its rearview mirror.

The following chart combines the US and euro-zone money supplies to create what we refer to as the G2 monetary inflation rate. The vertical red lines on this chart mark the starting times of the last three US recessions.

Like the Fed, the ECB is in monetary tightening mode in an effort to combat increases in prices caused mainly by supply issues. Therefore, the G2 monetary inflation rate probably will fall over the next few months.

Economically and monetarily, Australia and Canada are in similar situations. In both cases, the central bank is in monetary tightening mode because cost-of-living measures supposedly have risen too fast. Also, the residential housing market is weakening in both countries, which should result in less mortgage-related money creation by commercial banks.

In Australia’s case, new tax regulations that recently caused mortgage-related lending by commercial banks to drop sharply are weighing on the housing market and the monetary inflation rate. In Canada’s case, the housing market has been sluggish for years and is showing no signs of improvement.

With reference to the following charts, it’s reasonable to expect that the monetary inflation downward trends that began 9-12 months ago will continue over the next 6 months, adding downward pressure to house prices and helping to generate enough economic weakness to set the stage for central bank policy reversals by the middle of 2027.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is the only major central bank that currently is not leaning in the direction of monetary tightening. However, it also isn’t inflating aggressively. As illustrated below, China’s M1 money-supply growth rate has been making lower highs and lower lows since the start of 2010.

The direction of the next significant move in China’s monetary inflation rate will be important for gold and commodities, as it tends to influence prices in these markets with a variable lag. For example, a rise in China’s M1 growth rate to above the late-2025 high would eventually be supportive for the prices of gold and many other metals.

data.title: Analysts Raise Palantir Technologies Revenue, FCF And Stock Price Targets - Is PLTR Too Cheap?
data.description:
Analysts have raised their 2027 revenue forecasts for Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR), implying higher adjusted free cash flow (FCF). Price targets are also higher, despite PLTR's dip. Could PLTR be 38% too cheap here? This article discusses why that might be the case, and several ways to play PLTR.

PLTR closed at $163.59 on Wednesday, Nov. 25, ahead of Thanksgiving, up 1.50% for the day. That's up from a recent trough of $143.49 on Nov. 20, but still down over 21.7% from an Oct. 9 peak of $209.05. 

PLTR stock - last 6 months - Barchart - Nov. 25, 2026

Let's review what's happened since Palantir released its Q3 earnings.

Higher Revenue and Adj. FCF Forecasts

Palantir released its Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, 2026, showing strong revenue and adj. FCF growth and margins. I wrote about this in a Nov. 3 Barchart article, “Palantir Technology Shows Huge Unusual Call Options Activity - Is PLTR Stock Too Cheap?”

For example, in Q3, its adj. FCF margin was 52.3%, and management projected 2026 revenue of up to $8.534 billion and adj. FCF of $4.9b at the midpoint of its forecast range. That implies a 2026 adj. FCF margin of 57.4% (i.e., $4.9b/$8.53b).

Anthropic Bull vs Bear ETFs

Leveraged ETFs involve significant risks and are designed for short-term trading. Read the prospectus before investing. Distributor: ALPS Distributors, Inc.

Moreover, analysts now project even higher 2026 revenue of $8.55 billion. And for 2027, they forecast $13.14 billion (the prior forecast was $12.88 billion, as I discussed in my article).

As a result, if we assume at least a 55% adj. FCF margin (i.e., halfway between the Q3 margin and the estimated 2026 margin), Palantir should generate over $7 billion next year:

   $13.14b 2027 revenue est. x 0.55 = $7.227 billion adj. FCF

That's 47.5% higher than the 2026 adj. FCF forecast. As a result, PLTR could have a higher fair value.

Higher Palantir Valuation and PLTR Price Targets

In my last article, I used a 1.333% FCF yield to value Palantir's adj. FCF. That's because right now Palantir has a market cap of $392.17 billion, according to Yahoo! Finance:

   $4.9b 2026 est. adj. FCF / $394.17b = 0.0124 = 1.24% adj. FCF yield.

My higher 1.333% FCF yield metric is more conservative. For example, 1/0.0124 works out to an 80.6x multiple, whereas 1/.0133 has a lower 75.2x multiple.

Here is how that will work out using my new 2027 adj. FCF estimate:

  $7.227b 2027 adj. FCF x 75 = $542 billion fair value

That's over 38% higher than its existing $392 billion market cap today (as well as my prior $512 billion fair value estimate in the Nov. 3 Barchart article). That means the price target (PT) is higher:

  $163.59 price on Nov. 25 x 1.38 = $225.75 PT

That compares to my prior $208 PT. Moreover, analysts surveyed by Yahoo! Finance have raised their PTs as well: $222.90 today, vs. $216.00 on Nov. 3.

The result here is that analysts have raised their revenue forecasts, which automatically pushed up adj. FCF forecasts, as well as price targets.

Nevertheless, there's no guarantee PLTR won't keep falling. One conservative to play the stock is to sell short out-of-the-money (OTM) puts in nearby expiry periods.

Shorting OTM PLTR Puts

For example, the Dec. 31, 2026, expiry period shows that the $145.00 put option contract, over 11% below Wednesday's close, has a midpoint premium of $5.20.

PLTR puts expiring Dec. 31, 2026 - Barchart - As of Nov. 25, 2026

That means an investor who enters a trading order to “Sell to Open” this put, collects $520 upfront after posting $14,500 as collateral. 

So, the expected yield is 3.586%, assuming PLTR doesn't drop to $145.00 on or before Dec. 31.

However, note that even if that happens, the investor enjoys an attractive breakeven buy-in point: $145 - $5.20 = $139.80. That's 14.5% below the Nov. 25 closing price.

The risk is that if PLTR drops below $139.80, the investor owns 100 shares with an unrealized loss. The investor can then either wait or sell covered calls.

PLTR Put Credit Spread Play

Some investors, who have more risk tolerance, and don't want to post $14,500 in collateral, can buy a lower put, like the $135.00 strike price ($314 cost).

As a result, this put credit spread generates just $206 in collected income ($520-$314). However, the brokerage firm only requires $1,000 in collateral (($145-$135) x 100). So, the at-risk capital is just $794, with a much higher expected return:

  $206/$794 = 24.9% over 1 month

However, the risk is much higher. If PLTR drops to $135.00, the brokerage firm will debit 100% of the collateral. 

But consider this: the $135 strike price delta ratio is low, only -0.15. That implies an 85% chance PLTR won't drop to $135 by year-end.

Moreover, the investor can do 3 put credit spreads (i.e., to collect $618 with $2,382 at risk) to make a little more than the short-put play above. The benefit here is that only $3K collateral is required, or 21% of the $14.5K in the short-put play.

Summary and Conclusion

The bottom line is that PLTR looks even more attractive today after its Q3 earnings release. That's because analysts have raised their forecasts and PLTR stock has dipped. 

As a result, expected returns from out-of-the-money (OTM) PLTR option plays have risen.

data.title: Pound Has Chances To Close The Week With Moderate Gains
data.description:
GBP/USD is trading at 1.31026 on Friday. Despite attempts to recover during the week, the British currency continues to experience pressure from the dollar. Trading activity may remain subdued today due to the shortened post-Thanksgiving US session.

The main factor supporting the dollar remains the outlook for Fed monetary policy. PCE and third-quarter US GDP data published on Wednesday confirmed the stability of the American economy in the presence of high inflation. In addition to the expected 25 basis point rate hike in December, markets are pricing in two more increases in early 2027.

The geopolitical situation also contributes to sustained demand for the American currency. Recent statements by Donald Trump have provided no clarity on the prospects for an agreement with Iran, while the intensification of confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthis expands risks to the region's energy infrastructure.

At the same time, the potential for a further decline in the pound is limited by expectations of Bank of England policy tightening. Investors are increasingly pricing in a rate increase in December and expect this process to continue in 2027.

In the absence of significant macroeconomic data from the UK and the US, GBP/USD dynamics today will be determined mainly by geopolitical news and market sentiment. Despite current pressure, the pound has a chance to close the week with moderate gains for the first time in four weeks.

data.title: Is Oracle The Next Bear Stearns?
data.description:
The Bear Stearns Comparison

On Thanksgiving night, Michael Burry shared a piece with a striking comparison. In its November 20 analysis, Groundbreaker reported that five-year default protection on Oracle cost more than comparable protection on Bear Stearns at the start of 2008.

Groundbreaker’s argument starts with the rent. A developer borrows against what a tenant has promised to pay for a data center. If lenders grow less confident in that tenant, they’ll lend less against the same lease. Take a campus valued at $100 million with $85 million of debt. A 15% drop in its value wipes out the owner’s equity on paper. That can make the next campus harder to finance even if the tenant is still paying on time.

Three Days Versus Three Years

Bear Stearns borrowed against mortgage bonds, much of it overnight. As major lenders stopped renewing those loans, its pool of available cash and liquid assets went from about $18 billion on Monday to $2 billion on Thursday, as shown in a study of the run. That Thursday, it told the Fed it expected to come up short the next day.

Oracle, meanwhile, sold $10 billion in bonds and $10 billion in common stock on November 4. It agreed to pay 7% to 8.65% interest on the bonds, and the earliest of those bonds comes due in 2029, according to its SEC filing. On November 20, the same day Groundbreaker published, Oracle said it had secured the money it needed to fulfill its contract with OpenAI.

Oracle paid up for time and brought in new shareholders to bear part of the risk. It still needs OpenAI to pay for the computing capacity it signed up for. If those payments fall short, Oracle will owe the same interest on its new bonds with less cash coming in.

Who Has To Sell?

The places to look for a 2008-style run are the lenders and funds holding the debt. A lender with long-term funding may be able to hold a troubled loan while the borrower restructures. A fund facing margin calls or withdrawals may have to sell whatever it can, including investments unrelated to AI. Fed Governor Michael Barr singled out leveraged funds as a potential source of forced selling in an AI downturn.

Some losses could also land with the tech companies that helped finance their customers. At a TeraWulf campus in Kentucky, Google agreed to step in if Anthropic defaults on certain data-center leases. Google can pay the overdue rent and take over the lease or, in some circumstances, pay an exit fee. That protection kicks in when the last data hall on the relevant lease starts its term, according to TeraWulf’s filing.

For stock investors, we’d watch two things. First, are companies postponing campuses and chip orders as financing gets more expensive? That matters to Nvidia and its suppliers. Second, are lenders pulling funding from firms that hold AI debt? That’s how trouble at a data center can reach stocks that have nothing to do with AI.

Where We’re Looking Next

CoreWeave looks vulnerable if financing gets tighter. It spent $9.4 billion on capital investment in the third quarter and generated about $2 billion in operating cash flow, according to its latest earnings release.

We’re still bullish on AI names with stronger balance sheets. We’ve lined up a potential trade for today in one company we think could soon get an investment from the U.S. government.

data.title: Australia Inflation At 4.9%: What Drove It And Why The Australian Dollar Stayed Flat
data.description:
Australia inflation rose to 4.9% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 4.3% in September, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on 25 November. The trimmed mean, the underlying measure the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) uses, rose to 3.8%, and both figures beat forecasts. The Australian dollar closed the day almost where it started. This article breaks down what drove the jump, what it means for the RBA, why the currency barely moved and what the AUD/USD chart shows.

TL;DR

  1. Annual CPI rose to 4.9% in October from 4.3%; the trimmed mean rose to 3.8% from 3.6%. Forecasts were 4.7% to 4.8% and 3.6%.

  2. Housing and transport added 2.58 percentage points, a little over half of the 4.9%. Electricity rose 25.2% and automotive fuel 32.5%.

  3. AUD/USD closed at 0.6634 on 25 November, 0.06% above the day before. Analysts point to copper, the current account and a cooling economy; the next RBA meeting is on 7-8 December.

  4. On the four-hour chart AUD/USD trades in a descending channel. The educational scenario sells at 0.6710 with a stop at 0.6735 and a target of 0.6500.

Australia Inflation in October: The Numbers

The figure is the monthly consumer price index for October, released at 11:30 AEDT on 25 November. It is the annual rate over 12 months, and prices in October alone rose 0.5%, or 0.7% after seasonal adjustment.

Australia CPI for October 2026 against September and against forecasts

Sources: ABS for the results, FXStreet for the forecasts. The two forecasts for the headline differ by 0.1 point, and the result beat both.

What Is Behind the 4.9%

Two groups did most of the work. The ABS table of contributions shows how many percentage points each group added to the annual rate.

Housing and transport added 2.58 of the 4.9 points

Contribution to annual CPI, percentage points, 12 months to October 2026. Groups as published by the ABS.

Contribution of each group to Australia's annual CPI to October 2026, percentage points

  1. Housing prices rose 6.4%; the main contributors were electricity (+25.2%), new dwellings (+5.1%) and rents (+3.5%).

  2. Transport prices rose 10.6%; automotive fuel (+32.5%) was the main contributor.

  3. Food prices rose 3.5%; meals out and takeaway food (+4.1%) was the main contributor.

Values rounded from the ABS table (housing 1.3812, transport 1.1996). The groups shown add up to 4.62 points.

Source: ABS, Consumer Price Index, Australia, October 2026. Data as of 25 November 2026.

The two largest contributors are housing and transport, and the biggest price rises inside them are electricity and fuel. The ABS links the electricity rise to the end of last year's government rebates, which lowered bills a year ago, so part of the annual jump is a comparison with a subsidised base. Fuel follows the oil price. Together, housing and transport account for 2.58 points, about 53% of the annual rate by our arithmetic.

Why the Trimmed Mean Matters More for the RBA

The trimmed mean leaves out the items with the largest price moves each month, and fuel is outside it, which the ABS gives as the reason for the gap between 4.9% and 3.8%. The RBA uses this measure to judge underlying inflation.

In its November Statement on Monetary Policy, published after it raised the cash rate by 0.25 points to 4.85%, the RBA forecast headline inflation of 4.5% and a trimmed mean of 3.6% for December 2026. data.title: Rates Spark: Rates Resist Bearish Pressure As France Faces Rating Risk
data.description:
Bearish dynamics remain contained in European rates despite the ECB’s tightening bias and firmer energy prices. French spreads tightened ahead of S&P’s review, but political uncertainty and budget risks could warrant a negative outlook – and keep investors cautious

Bearish dynamics remain contained

Left on their own with the US out on holiday, European rates briefly tested the upside. While the European Central Bank accounts clearly pointed to the ECB’s tightening bias – maybe even beyond December – and energy prices also sneaked higher as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, a bearish dynamic failed to take hold in the end. What lingers is the uncertainty around the tech narrative.

S&P scheduled to review France after Friday’s market close

French bond spreads did manage to tighten over the past session, taking the 10y spread over Bunds below the 150bp threshold.

This seems to defy the risk of S&P lowering the outlook on the stable A+ rating it currently still attaches to France. Given the uncertain political backdrop, further budget slippage over the year and an eroding growth outlook, S&P may have enough reason to do just that. At the same time, it would no longer really come as a surprise. Fitch lowered the outlook of its A+ rating to negative at the end of October in an unscheduled move after having only just reviewed the country in August.

Moreover, markets are already pricing France more like a BBB-rated country. To be fair, much of this is likely an overshoot. In its recent Financial Stability Review, the ECB pointed to the procyclical role of hedge funds in eurozone government bond spread dynamics. At the same time, the lingering threat of a downgrade might create another hurdle for investors looking to return to the French bond market.

Replacing hedge fund demand may come at a costs to gilts

The Bank of England has reiterated its intention to introduce measures to strengthen the gilt repo market, which could negatively impact demand for gilts. Hedge funds have acted as an important marginal buyer over the past year, helping absorb the significant increase in gilt supply. A popular strategy is buying cash gilts and offsetting these positions with shorts in gilt futures, whereby repo markets offer the ability to leverage up such trades. The slight pricing difference between cash gilts and gilt futures can provide attractive returns. But if the repo costs were to rise, the attractiveness of such trades could fall.

In effect, hedge funds offer balance sheet capacity to house gilts, and therefore any headwinds to such trades can add upward pressure to gilt yields. But the impact is more nuanced. Because the gilt positions are hedged through futures, any unwind of the hedge fund positions should be relatively neutral in terms of term premium. We would, however, expect gilts to underperform swaps. The spread between swaps and gilts is strongly linked to the balance sheet costs of holding bonds. If hedge funds decide a trade is no longer attractive due to higher trading costs, then other players with higher balance sheet costs (such as banks) would have to jump in.

Friday's events and market view

We will see preliminary inflation data for November in France and Spain, where headline rates are expected to ease somewhat but remain at elevated levels. The ECB will also publish its consumer survey on expected inflation. ECB officials scheduled to speak are Chief Economist Philip Lane, Vice President Boris Vujčić, Germany's Joachim Nagel and France's Emmanuel Moulin.

In primary markets, Italy will auction 5y and 10y BTPS as well as 8y and 9y CCTeu floaters (in total up to 8bn).

data.title: Oil: The Market Has Already Written Off The Energy Crisis
data.description:
As investors turn their attention back to technology stocks, the market seems to believe that the oil crisis is now behind us. The spectacular drop in prices since October has helped reassure financial markets, which are anticipating a normalization of supply conditions and a retreat in inflationary pressures.

This complacency is dangerous. Behind the decline in paper oil prices, the fundamentals of the physical market continue to deteriorate. Inventories are falling, flows through the Strait of Hormuz are contracting again, and the structure of futures contracts points to mounting pressure on near-term supply.

From a technical perspective, WTI crude has been trading within a broad contracting triangle since March. The recent correction has formed a bullish harmonic pattern known as a Bullish Bat, whose completion point D coincides with the triangle’s lower boundary, around $80. Although the Fibonacci ratios do not perfectly match those of a textbook pattern, this convergence of technical support levels strengthens the likelihood of a rebound. The chart target for this move lies at the triangle’s upper boundary, in a zone between $98 and $102 per barrel. This bullish scenario remains valid as long as the ascending trendline support holds.

Inventories falling out of season

At this time of year, crude oil inventories normally tend to build as demand slows seasonally.

Yet the latest US statistics paint a very different picture. Total petroleum stocks fell by 5.3 million barrels in one week, despite another 2.9 million-barrel drawdown from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR):

Commercial crude inventories did increase by 1.1 million barrels, but total commercial stocks of petroleum and refined products fell by 2.4 million barrels.

US strategic reserves now contain just 273.5 million barrels.

The oil surplus that financial markets regularly talk about fails to materialize in the inventory data.

Hormuz: flows deteriorate again

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is deteriorating once more.

Oil flows through the strait have fallen back to around 6 million barrels per day on a seven-day average, compared with 20 million before the conflict:

More concerning still, a substantial gap is emerging between volumes loaded inside the Persian Gulf and those that actually make it through the strait.

Oil loadings in the Persian Gulf are running at nearly 16 million barrels per day, yet only 6 million barrels are currently passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

This gap suggests that oil is accumulating inside the Gulf, although the latest shipping data are preliminary and transit times need to be taken into account.

The market now appears convinced that Iran lacks both the means and the willingness to escalate the conflict. The absence of escalation around the Fujairah and Sohar transshipment hubs reinforces this view among traders.

But no one really knows Iran’s strategy – or its timeline.

The current status quo appears difficult to sustain. Any further escalation before year-end would come as political pressure on Donald Trump intensifies and oil reserve levels constrain the US room for maneuver.

The futures market is sending a warning signal

While oil prices have undergone a sharp correction, the spread between the first two Brent futures contracts has surged back to $3.82:

In practical terms, oil for delivery in January 2027 is trading $3.82 higher than oil for delivery in February.

This structure, known as backwardation, reflects a premium for immediate access to oil.

In a genuinely oversupplied market, one would expect the opposite. Traders would be incentivized to store oil and sell it later at a higher price.

Today, the market is instead rewarding prompt availability of barrels.

The spectacular decline in paper oil prices therefore masks persistent tightness in the front end of the curve.

Falling oil prices will not rescue the Fed

The compression of paper oil prices has an obvious political benefit: lowering inflation expectations and reassuring bond markets.

But the latest US inflation figures show the limits of this strategy.

The PCE index, the inflation gauge preferred by the Federal Reserve, continues to climb:

In October, US inflation measured by the PCE index reached 3.8% year-on-year, while core inflation, excluding energy and food, stood at 3.3% – well above the Fed’s 2% target.

Despite easing energy prices, underlying inflationary pressures are intensifying. US third-quarter growth has also just been revised up to 4.3% annualized.

Under these circumstances, the Fed is likely to raise rates in December. Markets are also anticipating another hike in January.

What happens if oil prices rise again while the Fed is already being forced to tighten monetary policy?

It’s not 2020 – but possibly 2022

Investors still seem to be thinking in terms of the 2020 scenario, when the collapse in financial markets triggered a historic drop in oil demand.

The current situation is radically different.

The main risk is not a collapse in demand, but a contraction in supply. In this respect, the comparison with 2022 seems far more relevant: equity markets can suffer sharp corrections while energy prices continue to rise.

Oil could therefore decouple from other financial assets during the next waves of equity-market liquidation.

If flows through Hormuz do not recover quickly, current prices could represent one of the last opportunities to buy a barrel below $100. In a scenario of prolonged shortages, that level could even become a floor in 2027.

The market has stopped paying attention to oil precisely when it should be watching it most closely.

The combination of another energy shock, persistent inflation and rising rates is likely to be one of the most underestimated risks facing financial markets as 2027 approaches.

Gold and the risk of another inflation shock

In the short term, the prospect of further Fed tightening and liquidity pressures could continue to weigh on gold prices. Over the medium term, however, another oil shock would confront central banks with a formidable dilemma: fighting inflation at the risk of triggering a financial crisis amid widespread excessive debt. Unlike in 2022, governments now have even less fiscal room to maneuver. Higher interest rates would substantially increase debt-servicing costs, while rising energy prices would undermine the real economy. It is precisely this monetary and fiscal predicament that reinforces gold’s appeal as a long-term protective asset.

data.title: Dell Delivers Record Results, But Wall Street Sees A Catch
data.description:
Dell Technologies delivered another record quarter, raised its annual forecasts and authorized billions in additional share buybacks. Yet Wall Street initially reacted by selling the stock.

Reuters reported Wednesday, Nov. 25, that Dell Technologies (DELL) shares fell 5.7% in early trading despite the company’s stronger outlook and an additional $25 billion share repurchase authorization. The stock later recovered, closing 0.6% higher at $297.06.

The erratic response followed the exceptional profits report.

Driven by the increasing demand for AI servers, Dell’s fiscal third-quarter sales more than doubled to a record $54.9 billion.

Additionally, the corporation revised its full-year sales prediction higher for the third time this year, from $192 billion to $202 billion.

Reuters reported Tuesday that the new forecast exceeded analysts’ expectations of approximately $194.5 billion.

However, the market’s initial reaction reflected growing apprehension about the massive expenditures required to sustain AI growth.

Investors are becoming more skeptical of technology firms’ ability to turn their infrastructure investments into long-term earnings.

For Dell shareholders, the tension is striking: The company is reporting record demand, but investors still want convincing evidence that the growth can last.

Dell’s AI server business delivers record results

Dell’s most recent financial results show how drastically AI has changed the company’s operations.

For the fiscal third quarter, the firm posted adjusted profits of $9.45 per share, which was higher than analysts’ projections of $6.59 and up 265% from the same period last year.

Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group generated $42 billion in revenue, representing a 198% annual increase, according to its Nov. 24 earnings release.

The company’s major financial highlights included:

  • Total revenue: $54.9 billion, up 103%.

  • AI server revenue: $22 billion, up 291%.

  • Traditional server and networking revenue: $15 billion, up 235%.

  • Storage revenue: $4.9 billion, up 24%.

  • Adjusted earnings per share: $9.45, up 265%.

  • AI server backlog: $132.3 billion.

Dell received $60.2 billion in AI server orders in the quarter, indicating continued computing infrastructure growth.

Jeff Clarke, COO, said the company evaluates orders based on customer quality, financing capacity, and infrastructure.

The large backlog gives Dell visibility into future demand, but orders must be fulfilled and revenue generated.

Why Wall Street remains cautious about Dell

Dell’s earnings come amid growing skepticism about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.

Reuters reported Wednesday that technology stocks faced renewed pressure as investors questioned the financing behind large data center expansions.

These worries have impacted businesses that provide servers, processors, and other equipment.

In addition, growing memory prices and concerns about future profitability put pressure on Dell.

The company’s infrastructure operating margin reached 17%, up from 12.4% a year earlier, although investors remain concerned about the outlook for hardware margins.

Another issue is Dell’s conventional PC business.

Although operating income fell by 6%, its Client Solutions Group’s sales increased by 3% to $12.9 billion.

Dell’s quarterly figures show that consumer PC sales dropped 15% to around $1.6 billion.

The disparity shows how much business infrastructure investment, as opposed to regular PC customers, now drives Dell’s growth.

Dell’s $25 billion buyback sends a different message

Dell’s management is expressing confidence in the company’s financial prospects, despite the market’s initial pessimism.

The board expanded its current buyback program by approving an extra $25 billion in share repurchases.

Dell also returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders through dividends and repurchases during the quarter.

Dell has not yet acquired $25 billion worth of shares as a result of the expanded authorization. Over time, it increases management’s ability to buy back shares.

Although the financial advantages depend on purchase price and execution, buybacks may reduce the number of outstanding shares and perhaps increase per-share profits.

Although the permission is a positive signal for investors, the dangers associated with future AI expenditure remain.

What Dell’s latest forecast means for shareholders

Dell now expects fiscal 2027 AI server revenue of $78 billion, up from its previous $74 billion forecast.

The company also raised its adjusted annual earnings outlook to $29.68 per share from $25.50.

Fourth-quarter revenue is projected to reach approximately $56.3 billion, with adjusted earnings of $8.40 per share.

These numbers imply that management anticipates a continued high demand for AI infrastructure.

The next challenge, meanwhile, is whether Dell can maintain its profitability while fulfilling a record backlog and controlling growing component prices.

Wednesday’s trade reflected that uncertainty.

Despite its remarkable performance, Dell first sold off, but by the closing bell, it had recovered.

The question of whether Dell can profit from the AI boom is no longer the most important for investors. The question now is whether the business can continue to develop profitably enough to meet Wall Street’s demands.

data.title: SpaceX Stock Surges 7.5%: Could Elon Musk's Giveaway Spark A Bigger Rally?
data.description:
• SpaceX stock rose 7.5% overnight as Elon Musk expanded his share giveaway.

  • The FCC approved SpaceX’s plan to deploy up to one million AI satellites.

  • Analysts’ average SpaceX price target implies 108% upside from Wednesday.

SpaceX stock Nasdaq: SPCX surged nearly 7.5% in overnight trading on Friday after Elon Musk expanded his commitment to distribute shares to American children.

The shares gained 7.47% on alternative trading platform Blue Ocean ATS, according to CNBC. SpaceX had closed 1.3% higher at $127.44 on Wednesday, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Elon Musk's latest pledge comes as the company secures regulatory approval for an ambitious orbital data centre project and accelerates investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Elon Musk's giveaway could create a generation of shareholders

Elon Musk has pledged to give American children an additional SpaceX share annually, extending an initial giveaway estimated to be worth around $18 billion.

SpaceX announced on Wednesday that it would issue one Class A share to each currently active Trump Account, with Musk personally matching the company's contribution.

The corporate distribution is expected in December, while Musk's personal contribution is scheduled for June 2027, following the expiration of his share lock-up period.

Assuming 72 million children receive one share annually, Musk's recurring donation would be worth approximately $9.2 billion at Wednesday's closing price. However, the actual value would depend on eligibility and prevailing market prices.

“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at Mitrade Group, told Reuters.

For existing shareholders, the distinction between the two contributions matters. Newly issued corporate shares dilute existing ownership, whereas transfers from Musk's personal holdings do not increase the outstanding share count.

Orbital data centres could reshape SpaceX stock's growth prospects

Beyond the giveaway, SpaceX secured permission from the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy up to one million satellites for its proposed Starmind orbital computing network.

The project could eventually reduce dependence on terrestrial electricity networks by using solar energy to power computing infrastructure in space.

SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033 and deploy at least 100,000 satellites by November 2035 under the regulatory authorisation.

Its rocket manufacturing and launch capabilities could give the company an advantage over competitors that rely on external launch providers.

Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu described SpaceX's launch business as its “core competitive advantage”, according to Investing.com. The brokerage initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $210 price target on Monday.

Meanwhile, the company's terrestrial computing expansion continues.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs announced the pricing of approximately $44 billion in financing for graphics processors and related equipment last week.

However, the orbital project's commercial viability remains unproven, with considerable engineering and financing challenges ahead.

SpaceX stock today: Wall Street sees substantial upside

SpaceX remains below its June initial public offering price of $135, based on Wednesday's regular-session close, despite strong earnings growth.

Third-quarter revenue increased 161% to $14.6 billion, while the company reported net income of $4.4 billion against a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.

Its Super Intelligence division generated $7.56 billion in revenue, accounting for more than half of group sales.

Baron Capital founder Ron Baron believes SpaceX's data centres could generate more than $50 billion in annual rental revenue, according to Benzinga.

The average price target of $265 among analysts tracked by TipRanks implies approximately 108% upside from Wednesday's close.

However, substantial AI investment requirements, potential shareholder dilution and uncertainty surrounding a possible Tesla merger remain risks.

data.title: HPE Plunges Despite Raising The Bar For 2027
data.description:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise delivered exactly what the bulls were looking for after a punishing month for AI hardware: a clean beat, an above-the-range quarter, and a fiscal 2027 outlook that blew past where analysts had been modeling.

The stock's reaction was more complicated. Shares rallied 17% during Monday's regular session as technology stocks surged, then gave back all of the gain – and then some – to drop below $40 per share in early Wednesday trading.

A Beat on Every Line That Matters

Adjusted earnings came in at $1.43 per share, topping the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.29 by nearly 11% and clearing the top of management's own $1.20 to $1.30 range. That compares with $0.62 a year ago. Revenue rose 50% to $14.55 billion, edging past consensus, and HPE has now topped the Zacks consensus on earnings in each of the last four quarters.

Fiscal 2026 as a whole was transformational. Revenue grew 36% to $46.7 billion, adjusted earnings reached $3.97 per share, and free cash flow climbed to $4.5 billion from less than $1 billion the year before. Antonio Neri described HPE as "a fundamentally different company, with greater earnings power," and the numbers certainly back up the corporate language.

The Guidance Is the Story

The fourth quarter was good. The fiscal 2027 outlook was something else entirely. In September, management laid out a framework calling for revenue growth of 13% to 17% and earnings growth of 16% to 20%. On Monday evening, the company raised revenue growth to 27% to 35%, or $59.4 billion to $63.1 billion, and set adjusted EPS at $5.05 to $5.35.

Put those numbers next to the Street. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2027 stood at $4.74 per share on $55.12 billion in revenue, so the low end of the new range sits about 6.5% above consensus and the midpoint nearly 10% above it. First-quarter guidance of $1.30 to $1.40 compares with a consensus of $1.10. The midpoint of the annual range implies growth of about 31% on top of a year in which earnings nearly doubled.

Expect estimate revisions to move sharply higher over the next week, which is precisely the dynamic the Zacks Rank rewards; HPE (HPE - Free Report) entered the report as a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Servers Carried the Quarter

Server revenue nearly doubled, up 94.7% to $8.8 billion, as the hyperscaler inferencing deal and the AI systems backlog converted to shipments. By my arithmetic, servers accounted for close to 90% of the company's year-over-year revenue increase and roughly 60% of total revenue.

Networking, the segment management has been touting, grew a more modest 12.3% to $3.1 billion, toward the top of management's 11% to 13% guide. Security slipped 1.8%. Networking operating margin eased to 22.1% from 23.4% a year ago.

The forward indicators were stronger: networking orders more than doubled, and networks-for-AI orders hit a record $1.2 billion in the quarter, with Neri putting the fiscal-year total in the "mid-$2 billion" range, inside the target he set. For fiscal 2027, management is targeting $7.5 billion to $8 billion of cumulative networks-for-AI orders, weighted to the back half as AMD Helios and Oracle deployments ramp.

None of that is a problem. But the segment outlook management gave on the call confirms that the 2027 upgrade leans more heavily on AI compute than on the Juniper pivot: Cloud & AI revenue is guided to grow 30% to 40%, against high-teens to low-20s growth for networking. Server demand is the more cyclical of the two.

Margins Held Up Better Than Feared

The margin picture is a quiet win. Non-GAAP gross margin stepped down to 38.2% from a record 40.4% in the third quarter, which was expected given the size and mix of the hyperscaler shipments, but it was still up 180 basis points from a year ago. More telling, Cloud & AI operating margin reached 18.4%, double the 9.3% of a year earlier and well above the mid-teens rate management had flagged.

The catch came on the call. Management guided Cloud & AI operating margin to about 14% for fiscal 2027, well below the 18.4% just reported, and said gross margin should moderate as the year progresses, driven by mix and the timing of large AI systems ramps. Marie Myers was candid: "we do expect to see some pressure in pricing."

Why the Stock Slipped

The post-release slide has a clearer explanation. The 17% Monday-session rally front-ran much of the good news, and the call then introduced two less comfortable details.


Image Source: StockCharts

The first is the margin step-down described above. The second came from a J.P. Morgan question: spread evenly, the fiscal 2027 networks-for-AI order target implies roughly flat quarterly orders versus the $1.2 billion just booked.

Management pointed to scale-out, scale-across and Helios networking trays as upside, but the arithmetic is fair. Neither undermines the guidance, but both temper how far investors should extrapolate one blockbuster quarter.

Bottom Line

At under $40, HPE trades at less than nine times the midpoint of its fiscal 2027 earnings guidance, a multiple that still prices in a great deal of skepticism.

Neri made the point himself on the call: "I don't see us at a multiple that is 8x-9x." The concentration in servers and the coming margin moderation are legitimate reasons for some caution. But a record $10.5 billion AI backlog, orders up 88%, a guide well above consensus and rising cash returns, all at a single-digit multiple, is not a stock I would be selling into this week’s downturn.

data.title: Gold Confidence Needs Rebuilding
data.description:
Gold prices remain under pressure for now, and it likely won’t settle until the current bout of market-wide selling eases.

Two things are pulling gold lower at this same time. The first is policy. Talk of U.S. interest rate hikes, a stronger dollar and climbing bond yields have pushed gold down to its lowest level since September 2025. Gold pays no interest and looks less appealing whenever safer, interest-paying assets get more attractive (US 10-year government bonds currently offer a fraction under 5%). The second driver of the move lower is liquidity. A tech-led sell-off over the last two months has set off fresh selling across the gold market, as investors cash in their winners to cover losses elsewhere.Supports, like worries over the ever-increasing US debt and steady buying from China, are likely to get pushed aside for now as sellers continue to shape market conditions.

The good news is that there are a few things that could turn the tide. If tech/AI steadies, the forced selling should ease. If inflation cools, helped along by cheaper oil, it will take much of the heat out of the December rate-hike chatter. Traders are keeping a close eye on the $3,500/oz. area, the next psychological support level after $4,000/oz. was broken.

Gold Weekly Chart (TradingView)

Looking ahead over the next six to twelve months, consolidation at current levels, followed by a mild move higher, if the Fed holds steady and eventually cuts in 2027, should see real yields drop and see investors moving back into gold. Central banks, especially the Bank of China, are likely to keep snapping up gold on dips, which should soften any falls and firm up support. The main risk is a Fed that stays hawkish for longer than anyone expects, which could leave gold stuck in a range for a while.

data.title: Thanksgiving Inflation, The Fed’s Debt Trap, And Gold’s Eastward Shift
data.description:
In the latest Money Metals Midweek Memo, host Mike Maharrey connects the rising cost of Thanksgiving dinner to a larger problem facing the U.S. economy: persistent inflation, record debt, and a Federal Reserve caught between fighting rising prices and keeping a debt-heavy economy afloat.

Maharrey also examines the recent sell-off in gold and silver, the scramble for liquidity on Wall Street, and surging Chinese gold demand. His central argument is that short-term pressure on precious metals has not erased gold’s long-term case.

Thanksgiving Dinner Costs Rise 6% in 2026

A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people is expected to cost an average of $58.63 this year, about 6% more than in 2025, according to the Farm Bureau. The organization has tracked grocery prices for 40 years, using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

That increase is nearly double the roughly 3.5% inflation rate measured by the Consumer Price Index, Maharrey noted. It also ends a three-year trend of falling Thanksgiving meal costs.

The longer-term comparison looks different. Since 2012, the cost of a traditional Thanksgiving dinner has risen about 18.5%, while cumulative CPI inflation has reached roughly 49%. Since October 2021, food prices in the CPI’s “food at home” index have climbed 22%, compared with an increase of about 10% for the traditional Thanksgiving meal.

Maharrey said the difference reflects how inflation moves unevenly across the economy. Supply and demand affect individual prices, while grocery stores may discount turkey and other holiday staples to bring customers in. Those changing prices can coexist with a general rise in the overall price level.

Inflation Compounds Even When It Cools

Maharrey cautioned that slower inflation does not mean prices are falling. It means they are rising at a slower pace. Even the Federal Reserve’s 2% inflation target compounds over time, steadily reducing the purchasing power of money.

Inflation, Maharrey argued, has remained above 2% for 68 consecutive months. He questioned whether policymakers can bring it down to target without damaging an economy weighed down by government, corporate, and consumer debt.

The debate has become central to the outlook for gold and silver. Maharrey said market commentary has focused on expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December and keep rates higher for longer. He argued that this view often overlooks the strain higher borrowing costs place on an already indebted economy.

The Federal Reserve’s Inflation and Debt Dilemma

The episode framed the policy debate as a Fed “catch-22.” Higher interest rates may help restrain inflation, but they also make it more expensive to service debt and can put pressure on businesses and consumers.

Maharrey cited U.S. national debt above $40.5 trillion, with the total approaching $40.7 trillion and potentially reaching $41 trillion within the next month or two. He also pointed to more than $1 trillion in annual federal interest expense, rising small-business bankruptcies, and consumers struggling with high-interest credit card debt.

Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman has warned that continued rate hikes could push the United States into recession. In a post on X, Ackman called further increases another mistake and said financial conditions had already tightened sharply. Maharrey cited SpaceX securing debt financing at 8.25%, compared with a 6% rate on its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO in June.

Maharrey also cited small-business bankruptcies rising 46% during the first nine months of 2026 and an increase in delinquent auto loans as signs of financial strain. In his view, rate hikes could intensify pressure across an economy carrying heavy debt loads.

Ackman has argued that a 3% inflation target may be more realistic in a world shaped by geopolitical risk, military spending, tariffs, deglobalization, and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and energy. Maharrey challenged the idea that a higher target solves inflation, arguing that it would instead accept a faster loss of purchasing power.

Years of Easy Money Complicate the Fed’s Choices

Maharrey traced the current dilemma to years of monetary stimulus. After the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve held rates near zero for almost a decade. A limited attempt to normalize rates in 2018 was followed by rate cuts and renewed quantitative easing.

By the time the COVID-19 pandemic began, the Fed had already cut rates three times and expanded its balance sheet. During the pandemic, it brought rates back to zero and injected nearly $5 trillion into the economy through quantitative easing.

When the Fed began raising rates in March 2022, the change helped trigger a banking crisis, Maharrey said. He argued that this history shows how difficult it may be to withdraw monetary support without causing significant economic stress.

Maharrey believes that, when forced to choose between fighting inflation and supporting the economy during a crisis, the Federal Reserve has historically chosen stimulus. He expects the central bank could eventually cut rates and expand money creation again, even if that means renewed inflationary pressure.

Why Gold and Silver Have Fallen

Gold was trading below $3,500 an ounce as Maharrey recorded the episode, nearly $2,000 below its January high. He described himself as short-term bearish on precious metals, while maintaining that the growing debt burden supports gold’s longer-term outlook.

One factor behind the sell-off, he said, is a scramble for liquidity. As investors sell assets to raise cash, gold and silver can fall alongside stocks, even though precious metals are often viewed as safe havens. Investors may sell highly liquid gold to cover margin calls or exit losing trades.

Maharrey pointed to similar behavior during the early stages of the 2008 financial crisis and the pandemic. In his view, gold’s initial decline during market stress does not necessarily signal that its safe-haven role has disappeared.

Chinese Gold Demand Surges as Western Investors Sell

While Western investors have been selling, Chinese buyers have continued accumulating gold. China imported 155.9 metric tons in October, up 174% from October 2025. The value of China’s gold imports reached a record $29 billion so far in 2026, and gold was the country’s third-largest import category in October.

Gold withdrawals from the Shanghai Gold Exchange also strengthened during a month when they typically ease. Withdrawals rose 2% month over month to 94 tons in October, according to the World Gold Council. Maharrey said dip buying and strong bullion sales helped drive the increase.

He also noted speculation that higher gold imports could help reduce the appearance of China’s large trade surplus by increasing the value of imports. More broadly, he described a pattern in which price weakness in Western markets has coincided with continued gold accumulation in China and India.

Trading-hour data cited in the episode showed gold rising 12.9% during Asian trading hours in the first six months of the year, while falling 15% during North American trading hours. Gold declined 1.3% during European hours over the same period. Maharrey said the pattern points to a shift in gold flows from Western markets toward Asia, where new infrastructure is also being developed to challenge Western dominance in gold trading.

Maharrey’s Outlook: Short-Term Volatility, Long-Term Inflation Risk

Maharrey’s outlook combines caution about the near term with a bullish long-term view of gold. Precious metals may remain under pressure as investors seek liquidity and markets respond to interest-rate expectations. But he argues that heavy debt, the limits of monetary tightening, and the possibility of renewed stimulus continue to support gold’s long-term role as an inflation hedge.

As the holiday season begins, Maharrey also highlighted gold and silver as potential gifts, describing them as tangible assets that can be held over time. He directed listeners to Money Metals for precious metals products, market news, and information about buying, selling, and storing bullion.

data.title: No Groundhog Day, No Cold Turkey: Wall Street's Thanksgiving Bounce Gives The AI Bulls Something To Chew On
data.description:
No Groundhog Day, and Thankfully No Cold Turkey

No Groundhog Day, and thankfully no cold turkey either. Investors appear to have used Thanksgiving as an opportunity to treat this week’s apparent double bottom as a chance for retail to continue rummaging through the carnage and pick up a few cheap AI stocks for their portfolios. After a November that has put even the most hardened technology bulls through the wringer, the hope is that the underlying fundamentals will eventually reassert themselves and, more importantly, that the worst of the liquidation has finally run its course.

That is certainly a more encouraging proposition than another day of watching the Nasdaq surrender an early recovery and head straight back into the basement. But I wouldn’t get too carried away with Thursday’s price action. With US cash markets closed and much of Wall Street operating with holiday staffing, the overseas session feels like a pass-the-rally-baton day rather than a genuine test of institutional conviction. I suspect a fair number of senior traders and risk managers have already called it a week and won’t be back at their desks until Monday.

Nonetheless, the market’s willingness to look beyond the immediate carnage is encouraging. Investors in Europe and Asia took their cue from Wednesday’s late recovery on Wall Street, when bargain hunters dragged the Nasdaq 100 back from the brink of a bear market after another extraordinary session of intraday swings.

But as I’ve been suggesting, the underlying market data tell a more interesting story. The pre-Thanksgiving turnaround and the overnight extension appear to be getting an additional lift from the unwinding of US equity downside hedges, creating a mechanical bid through the derivatives market as dealers adjust their bearish exposures. That is not only helping restore risk appetite but also putting a bid under the “ Big Board” sectors that have been under the cosh.

But there’s an important distinction between a rally driven by hedging-flow unwinds and one supported by genuine institutional buying. The former can move markets significantly, particularly when liquidity is thin, but the real test comes when Wall Street’s skeleton-thin holiday desks return to full force.

Europe’s Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7%, while the MSCI Asia Pacific Index climbed 0.8%, marking only its second advance in eleven sessions. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures added about 0.5%, suggesting that, for now at least, investors are willing to give the rebound the benefit of the doubt.

The improvement was particularly evident across Asian technology markets. South Korea’s SK Hynix (SKHY) and Japan’s Kioxia outperformed, while technology-heavy benchmarks in Taiwan and South Korea advanced more than 2%. European technology shares also gained more than 2%, although the broader regional rally was led by automobile manufacturers and mining stocks.

For South Korea, the timing of Wall Street’s rebound could hardly have been better. Seoul had already been scrambling to contain the fallout from the US-led rout in AI and semiconductor shares, with authorities temporarily easing daily corporate share-buyback limits for three months starting November 24 and launching an intensified crackdown on illegal short selling. The measures stopped short of an outright short-selling ban or direct government purchases of equities, despite short-selling turnover reaching roughly 23 trillion won between November 2 and 20, with foreign investors accounting for more than 75% of the activity.

Fortunately for Seoul, the Wall Street recovery gave Korean shares a timely lift before investors had much opportunity to test the latest page in the country’s ongoing plunge-protection playbook.

Regardless, that’s a reasonably constructive response to Wednesday’s late buying, especially after the beating technology investors have absorbed since the US midterm elections. Leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) added another layer of uncertainty to an already uncomfortable market, pushing major equity benchmarks into correction territory and leaving traders struggling to distinguish a genuine recovery from another short-lived bounce.

At least Thursday’s response suggests the selling pressure has eased. Whether that translates into a sustained recovery is another matter, especially when much of the Wall Street crowd that normally sets the tone is probably more interested in turkey and football than adjusting its risk limits.

Sentiment Took the Beating. The Fundamentals May Have Survived.

A more constructive argument emerging from the wreckage is that investors spent much of November punishing technology shares for risks that haven’t materially changed underlying earnings and the investment outlook.

AI capital expenditure remains substantial, access to financing has not disappeared, and pricing power across some of the industry’s most important companies remains exceptionally strong. The damage has been concentrated in investor confidence, positioning and valuations rather than a wholesale deterioration in the businesses themselves.

That is essentially the case the bargain hunters are making.

After such a sharp adjustment in technology valuations, investors are beginning to ask whether the selling has gone too far relative to the earnings outlook. And if the answer is yes, then the market doesn’t necessarily need a spectacular new catalyst to recover. Sometimes it simply needs the forced sellers to finish selling and the remaining investors to rediscover a little confidence.

The apparent double bottom has therefore arrived at an interesting moment. Wednesday’s recovery didn’t erase November’s damage, but it suggested buyers are becoming more willing to absorb supply rather than stand aside and wait for another leg lower.

There are also some encouraging signs beyond technology. Copper recovered nearly 1% from an eleven-month low, Brent crude climbed above $96 a barrel for the first time in more than a week, and European government bonds weakened as demand for traditional havens eased.

Those moves suggest the improved risk appetite isn’t confined to a handful of semiconductor names. The participation of cyclical shares and commodities gives the rebound more credibility, although one holiday session is hardly enough evidence to declare the correction finished.

And therein lies the distinction. Fundamentals don’t need to have deteriorated for the market to have fallen too far, but a recovery in sentiment doesn't automatically mean the coast is clear.

The Fed Hasn’t Gone Away for Thanksgiving

Despite the renewed enthusiasm around the AI trade, one rather awkward guest is still at the Thanksgiving table: the Federal Reserve.

The prospect of another interest-rate increase in December remains a headwind for equities, particularly after a month in which investors have been repeatedly reminded that higher financing costs and crowded positioning can be an uncomfortable combination.

The S&P 500 is threatening to match one of its choppiest trading stretches since the 2022 bear market, and while Wednesday’s recovery was impressive, nothing obvious changed the outlook. Buyers simply emerged late in the session, apparently deciding that the damage had become excessive.

That is not necessarily a bad thing. Markets frequently turn before the news improves, and waiting for an official invitation to buy usually means arriving after everybody else has taken the best seats.

But it does leave the recovery with something to prove.

For now, the credit market has held up well enough to suggest equity volatility hasn’t developed into a broader financial problem. That is encouraging, particularly while economic growth and corporate earnings remain reasonably resilient. If the Fed ends its tightening cycle next year, there is still a plausible path to further equity gains.

The immediate difficulty is that the Fed hasn’t finished its work, and the latest technology rebound has done little to change that calculation.

The market may have found a reason to stop selling, but it hasn’t yet been given a particularly compelling reason to start chasing.

That is why the next couple of sessions matter, although I wouldn’t place too much emphasis on Friday’s shortened US trading day. Holiday liquidity can exaggerate moves in either direction, and with many senior traders likely extending their Thanksgiving break, the more meaningful test may not arrive until Monday.

That’s when the larger risk books return to something resembling normal participation, and portfolio managers must decide whether Wednesday’s apparent double bottom justifies rebuilding exposure.

The Turkey Is on the Table. The Verdict Can Wait Until Monday.

For now, investors have something to be thankful for. Wednesday’s late-session buying rescued the Nasdaq 100 from a deeply uncomfortable position, and Thursday’s response across Europe and Asia suggests that the appetite for beaten-down technology shares hasn’t disappeared.

The recovery also has a reasonable fundamental argument. Corporate earnings haven’t suffered the deterioration implied by some of the recent price action, AI investment expectations remain strong, and valuations have become more appealing after November’s sharp correction.

But there is still a difference between recognizing an opportunity and declaring the correction finished.

With the Fed’s December decision approaching, market volatility remains elevated, and much of Wall Street is away for Thanksgiving; Thursday’s advance deserves respect without being mistaken for a definitive change in direction.

My sense is that investors are beginning to treat the apparent double bottom as an opportunity to rebuild some exposure, rather than automatically viewing every bounce as another chance to sell. That’s an encouraging change in behaviour, even if the evidence remains preliminary.

And perhaps that is all we need to take away from this Thanksgiving session. After weeks of violent reversals, the market has finally managed to string together a little optimism without immediately handing it all back. Asia and Europe have followed Wall Street’s lead, a few AI cheapies are returning to portfolios, and the immediate urge to liquidate appears to have faded.

Not a bad outcome after the week we’ve had.

But with the senior dealing desks largely empty, I’d rather wait until Monday before deciding whether the market has genuinely found its feet or simply enjoyed a rather pleasant Thanksgiving holiday.
