data.title: Asia Week Ahead: RBI Rate Hike, And Data On China, Japan, Korea
data.description:
Markets will watch the Reserve Bank of India’s expected 25bp rate hike, while keeping a close eye on China’s PMIs, activity indicators from Japan and South Korea, Philippine inflation data, and Taiwan’s local elections.

India: RBI to hike rates 25bp amid persistent inflation

We expect the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to raise its policy rate by 25bp on Friday, as both headline and core inflation have moved above the central bank’s target, strengthening the case for further tightening. While lower fuel prices should ease headline inflation in the months ahead, food remains a key concern in India. It poses upside risks to inflation expectations and keeps underlying price pressures elevated. As a result, core inflation is likely to remain relatively sticky.

Philippines: Headline inflation to ease as fuel prices fall

Philippine CPI inflation should ease further, reflecting sharp declines in fuel prices. Gasoline and diesel have recorded consecutive weekly cuts, with average gasoline prices down around 11% in November versus October, providing meaningful drag on headline inflation. Core inflation, however, is likely to remain relatively sticky, supported by still-firm services costs and underlying domestic demand.

China: Manufacturing to improve but remain in contraction

China published November purchasing managers’ index data. We’re looking for the manufacturing PMI to rebound to 49.5 in November, up from 49.3, but remain in contraction territory. Industrial production cooled slightly in October. Ideally, we’d see better momentum in November. The non-manufacturing PMI is expected to fare slightly better, coming in at 49.7, stable from October.

Taiwan: Local elections in focus

No significant data releases are expected for Taiwan in the week ahead. However, local elections over the weekend will be the key event to watch. Though these elections may often be driven more by local issues than national politics, they will still serve as a check on relative support for the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Kuomintang (KMT).

Korea: Trade strength and inflation in focus

South Korea will release October industrial production data on Monday. The market expects annual growth to accelerate to 14.5% year-on-year, from 1.2% in September. Month-on-month, output is forecast to decline 0.6% after the previous month’s 9.0% increase.

November trade data are due on Tuesday. Exports and imports are expected to grow 98.9% and 38.8% YoY, respectively, supported by robust semiconductor and AI-related demand. The trade surplus is forecast to widen to $48.6bn, from a revised $42.7bn in October.

Korea releases November CPI data on Wednesday. The market expects headline inflation to ease to 2.7% YoY, from 2.8% in October. Persistent above-target inflation would support the Bank of Korea’s continued tightening bias following its November rate hike.

Japan: Retail sales, IP and capital spending in focus

Japan releases October retail sales and industrial production data on Monday. The market expects retail sales growth to rise to 2.7% YoY, from a revised 2.4% in September. The improvement would suggest that household consumption is recovering gradually, although elevated living costs and higher borrowing costs remain headwinds. Industrial production is expected to rise 2.1% MoM in October, broadly in line with September’s 2.0% increase. Year-on-year, the market expects industrial production growth to accelerate to 2.7% from 1.7%, indicating that manufacturing activity remains resilient.

Japan will also release third-quarter capital spending data on Monday. The market expects capital spending growth to accelerate to 4.3% YoY, from 1.6% in the second quarter. The expected pickup would suggest that corporate investment remains resilient despite higher borrowing costs.

data.title: AI Off-Balance Sheet Financing Worries The Fed
data.description:
The October FOMC minutes contain a sentence worth discussing. Per the recently released minutes, the Federal Reserve staff :

highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, noting that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint.

We wrote about the circular financing half of that sentence two weeks ago in Nvidia Circular Financing. The leasing half deserves equal attention and has received very little media coverage.

Here is the leasing mechanism that worries the Fed. When a hyperscaler commits to a long-dated data center lease, accounting rules do not recognize the obligation until the lease commences. A company can therefore sign binding commitments for facilities that will not open for years and record no liability until then. They will disclose the future obligation in a footnote.

The leasing commitments are not small. Reporting on the filings of the five largest US hyperscalers puts combined future data center lease commitments nearing $1 trillion, of which roughly two-thirds sits off balance sheet. Meta alone discloses about $279 billion, none of it on its balance sheet, alongside a $28 billion residual value guarantee on leases beginning in 2029 that is also unrecorded.

So why should we care? Consider that the massive AI buildout is driving the economy today and promises significant future growth. The buildout is predicated on massive capital spending. This spending is increasingly coming from investors, not from cash flows. These investors should be aware that almost every financial leverage measure analysts, index providers, and rating agencies apply to these companies is calculated from balance sheets that omit most of the commitments.

The Fed minutes further noted:

Greater scrutiny of the sector’s returns and financing could lead to a slowing in AI-related spending.

The Fed appears to be contemplating a credit crunch if investors were to hold back on AI investments and the economic impact it could have on the entire economy.

What To Watch Today

Market Trading Update

On Wednesday, we used Nvidia’s round trip to explain the math of losses and noted that Monday’s 4.7% surge stalled just below the 200-day moving average. Today, I want to look underneath the index because market breadth is improving beneath a sloppy tape, and that matters more heading into December.

Last Friday was a genuine washout. Only 975 US-listed issues advanced against 4,014 decliners, and roughly 87% of dollar volume traded on the downside. The S&P 500 closed nearly three standard deviations below its 20-day average with RSI near 25.

Monday flipped that almost exactly, with 4,099 advancers, 655 decliners, and about 89% of dollar volume flowing into rising stocks. Paul Desmond’s work at Lowry Research tied pairs of 90% down days and 90% up days to selling climaxes. We came close to that pattern, though not quite.

Notice what happened next. The S&P 500 slipped on Tuesday and Wednesday, yet advancers beat decliners on both days, by nearly 3-to-1 on Wednesday. The catch is dollar volume. Only 38% and 42% of it flowed into rising stocks because the selling was concentrated in the mega-caps. To wit: the Nasdaq 100 briefly approached bear-market territory on Wednesday as Nvidia fell another 5%, while the S&P 400 midcaps gained about 1%.

The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) tells the story most clearly. It has reclaimed its 50-day moving average and sits only about 3% below its November 4 record high. The cap-weighted index, by contrast, remains roughly 8% off its October high and below its 200-day average near 7,348. Bob Farrell’s Rule #7 holds that broad markets are strong markets and narrow ones are fragile. Right now, the average stock is healing faster than the index, which is the opposite of a market that is breaking down.

Of course, the skeptic in the back row will point out that bear-market rallies also start with big up days. He’s right. Such is the problem with oversold bounces, since they all look identical on day one. The test I’m watching is Marty Zweig’s breadth thrust. The 10-day average of advancing stocks is near 40%, the launch point. A move above 61.5% within 10 sessions, which takes us into early December, would confirm that buyers are committing and not just covering shorts.

Here’s how we’re managing it. We trimmed technology on Tuesday and raised cash, and we are NOT chasing a holiday half-day with thin liquidity. We will redeploy in stages once the S&P 500 closes above its 200-day average and breadth confirms, favoring broad, equal-weight exposure over buying back the mega-cap “dip”. Friday’s low near 6,882 is the risk line. A close below it voids the healing thesis, and we will respect that.

The most convincing rallies are often the ones that fail.

The Black Friday Consumer Test

Consumer sentiment sits near a record low while consumers keep spending. The University of Michigan index registered 48.0 in October, the second weakest reading in the survey’s history, yet retail sales are running roughly 5% above last year. Black Friday will test which signal deserves more weight.

For starters, the hard data has held up much better than the consumer surveys. As we share below, other than in June and July, when consumers were shocked by higher gasoline prices, consumer spending has held up well. With rapidly declining gasoline prices, household confidence should improve and, with it, spending may pick up, including on Black Friday.

Forecasters cannot agree on what will happen this weekend. The National Retail Federation expects 182.7 million Thanksgiving weekend shoppers, fewer than last year. The International Council of Shopping Centers expects 237 million shoppers spending less, roughly $124 billion against $127 billion. Bain projects weekend sales up nearly 9%, and Adobe sees online spending rising 7.4%. Those are not small disagreements.

It is worth disclaiming that many consumers have already begun holiday shopping, so a meaningful share of the spending season has been pulled forward. A soft Friday may reflect timing rather than weakness, and a strong one may simply be borrowing from December.

Here is what we take from it. Sentiment surveys have insisted the consumer has been exhausted for well over a year, while spending carried on regardless. Until the hard data breaks, we would keep weighting what households do above what they say.

data.title: Jobless Growth: What A Shrinking Workforce Means For Investors
data.description:
Jobless growth is usually a symptom of a weak economy, but this time the economy is growing due to productivity gains even as the workforce shrinks, which changes what investors should watch.

Key Takeaways

  • Real GDP grew by 2.2% in the year to mid-2026 while payroll employment grew just 0.3%. That is jobless growth by any definition.

  • Past episodes of jobless growth came after recessions, with unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%. Today it’s happening mid-expansion with unemployment at 4.2%.

  • The workforce is shrinking. Participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% to 36.9% over the past year as boomers retire.

  • With fewer workers, growth has to come from productivity, which rose 2.2% over the past year, slightly above its long-run average of 2.0%.

  • For investors, weak payroll numbers alone are a poor recession signal now. Unemployment, layoffs, and the wealth effect matter more.

Here’s a combination that doesn’t usually last. Over the year to the second quarter of 2026, the U.S. economy grew 2.2% after inflation.1 Over roughly the same stretch, payroll employment grew 0.3%.2 Hiring averaged about 41,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, and four of those months were outright negative. Economists call this “jobless growth,” and it has a reputation as a warning sign.

The reputation is earned. Historically, jobless growth showed up after recessions, when companies squeezed more output from fewer workers and refused to hire until they had to. Add American Express announcing 3,500 job cuts on October 23 and the “recession is coming” crowd has plenty of material.3 However, when you look at who is actually leaving the labor force, this version of jobless growth tells a very different story, and it matters for how you read the next jobs report.

What Is Jobless Growth?

Jobless growth is exactly what it sounds like: the economy expands, measured by GDP, while employment barely moves. Normally, the two travel together because more output requires more workers. The chart below shows that relationship over six decades.

Notice in the chart above that the gold line usually tracks the black one. The gaps open in specific places: the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and the years after 2009. Each of those was a “jobless recovery.” Businesses had just lived through a recession, and demand was soft. Companies met rising orders by working existing staff harder rather than adding headcount.

Today’s gap looks similar on the surface. The difference is the unemployment rate sitting underneath it.

Source: BLS and BEA via FRED (GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE). Two-year changes from Q2 (GDP) and June (payrolls). Calculations: RIA Advisors.

The last two rows are almost identical in growth and hiring. In 2011, jobless growth meant millions of people wanted work and couldn’t find it. In 2026, it means there are fewer people looking. Such is the distinction most of the “jobless growth” coverage misses, and it changes the investment conclusion entirely.

Hiring Stalled, But Unemployment Didn’t Rise

If weak hiring reflected weak demand for workers, unemployment would be climbing. It isn’t.

The unemployment rate was 4.4% in September 2025 and 4.2% in September 2026.4 Over the same year, the civilian labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people, from about 171.3 million to 170.3 million.5 When the pool of workers is shrinking, an economy doesn’t need many new jobs to keep unemployment steady. Oxford Economics has estimated that the “break-even” pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment stable is now close to zero.6

“So a 30,000 jobs print is fine now?” In isolation, it’s far less alarming than it would have been when the labor force was still growing, and new workers needed new jobs. What hasn’t changed is the direction of travel. A shrinking number is still a shrinking number, and as I’ve written before in The Sahm Rule, Employment, And Recession Indicators, it’s the change in unemployment, not the level of hiring, that has historically marked the turn.

The Workers Are Disappearing, Not The Jobs

The biggest reason for the shrinking labor force is demographic, and it’s been building for years.

Participation among Americans 55 and older climbed from 32.3% in 2000 to a peak of 40.7% in 2013. The leading edge of the baby boom was working longer than prior generations.7 That cohort is now leaving. Participation fell to 36.9% in September 2026, down from 38.0% just a year earlier. Slower immigration adds to it. Oxford Economics expected net inflows could fall to as little as 160,000 a year, from more than 3 million a few years ago.6

This is where I part company with the view that jobless growth is primarily an AI story. AI is real, and it plays a role, but the arrow runs the other way. When the labor force stops growing, businesses have only two ways to keep expanding: move the work offshore or replace it with technology. Automation is the response to a shrinking workforce, not the sole cause of it. Both responses are disinflationary over time, which fits the broader case I made in Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn’t.

Where The Bears Have A Point

The other side of this argument has real merit. A “low-hire, low-fire” labor market is stable only as long as the “low-fire” part holds. Companies that aren’t hiring also aren’t building a cushion, and if layoffs start, there’s little momentum in hiring to absorb them.

“The labor market is the main firewall against a recession.” – Michael Pearce, Oxford Economics, quoted in Fortune, February 2026

There’s also a white-collar wrinkle. Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute found that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional services peaked in November 2022, even as output continued to rise. He called AI-enabled automation a “plausible contributor.”6 Those are well-paid jobs, and their incomes drive a disproportionate share of consumer spending. Throw in four negative payroll months in the past year, and the bears aren’t making things up. They’re reading the same data I am. They just draw a darker conclusion from a pattern that, so far, has kept unemployment near 4%.

Can Productivity Carry The Economy?

The math of growth is simple. Output equals the number of workers times what each one produces. If the first number is flat or falling, everything rides on the second.

As shown, productivity rose 2.2% over the year to the second quarter of 2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965.8 That’s healthy, but it isn’t a boom, and it sets a ceiling. An economy with a flat workforce and 2% productivity growth has a speed limit of roughly 2% real growth, no matter what the AI headlines promise.

That ceiling matters for both sides of the market. For corporations, producing more with the same headcount improves margins. For households, it’s a mixed bag. Total wage income grows more slowly when the number of wage earners isn’t growing. Consumer spending then leans harder on raises for existing workers and on the stock market. Economist Byron Gangnes at the University of Hawaii estimated in October that the AI buildout’s direct contribution to growth has been small. The bigger effect, he found, has come through the stock market’s wealth effect on spending.9 I covered how fragile that channel can be in Wealth Effect Increases And Recession Risks.

“Jobless growth used to mean nobody was hiring. Now it means nobody is left to hire, and that is a very different problem.”

What Jobless Growth Means For Investors

I’m reasonably confident the shrinking labor force is a multi-year trend, not a blip. Boomers aren’t coming back to work. That makes jobless growth more likely to be the norm than the exception for the rest of this decade. What I’m less confident about is how smoothly the economy adjusts. A market that depends on asset prices for consumer spending is only as stable as those prices.

A few practical points follow from that view. First, stop reading weak payroll numbers as a recession signal on their own. With break-even job growth near zero, the unemployment rate and jobless claims are far better gauges. Second, separate the economy from earnings. Productivity-driven growth can support corporate margins even when hiring is flat. Third, keep an eye on the consumer. When incomes grow slowly, spending becomes more sensitive to a drop in the stock market, and that feedback loop runs in BOTH directions.

The trade-off is real. In my view, a disinflationary, slower-growth backdrop tends to favor high-quality bonds over aggressive growth bets, but it also means an economy with less room for error if a shock arrives. Such is the price of growing without new workers: steadier inflation, thinner cushions.

Bottom Line

Today's jobless growth reflects a shrinking workforce more than a collapsing economy, so investors should watch unemployment, productivity, and the wealth effect rather than the payroll headline.

The economy can keep growing without new workers. It just can’t afford to lose the ones it has.

Questions This Article Answers

What is jobless growth?

Jobless growth is a period in which the economy expands, measured by real GDP, while employment barely rises. In the year to mid-2026, real GDP grew by 2.2% while payroll employment grew 0.3%. Historically, it appeared after recessions, in the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and after 2009.

Is jobless growth a sign of a coming recession?

Not on its own. Past episodes saw unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%, but in 2026 unemployment was 4.2% and falling, as the labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people. A rising unemployment rate is a more reliable warning sign than weak hiring.

Why is the US labor force shrinking?

Baby boomers are retiring, and immigration has slowed. Labor force participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% in September 2025 to 36.9% in September 2026, down from a peak of 40.7% in 2013.

How can the economy grow without adding jobs?

Through productivity, meaning more output per hour worked. Nonfarm productivity rose 2.2% in the year to mid-2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965. With a flat workforce, that productivity rate sets a rough ceiling on real growth.
